title: Chain Rule
body:
[[Multivariable Chain Rule]]

---

$$
\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}
$$

**Differentiate the outside leaving the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the
inside.** It is the rule for compositions, and it is the only [[Differentiation Rules|rule]] in
Calc 1 that the rest of the degree genuinely depends on.

The Leibniz form is the one to think in, because it says what the rule *means*: if $y$ changes
three times as fast as $u$, and $u$ changes twice as fast as $x$, then $y$ changes six times as
fast as $x$. Rates multiply along a chain. The $du$'s appear to cancel, and
[[Linear Approximation]] is the reason that bookkeeping is legitimate rather than a coincidence.

## Worked

$$
y = (3x^2 + 1)^5
$$

```
outside:  u⁵        →  5u⁴          leave the inside alone
inside:   3x² + 1   →  6x
                                     y' = 5(3x² + 1)⁴ · 6x = 30x(3x² + 1)⁴
```

Nested compositions just extend the chain. $\sin(e^{x^2})$ peels one layer at a time:
$\cos(e^{x^2}) \cdot e^{x^2} \cdot 2x$.

The commonest error is stopping early: writing $5(3x^2+1)^4$ and forgetting the $6x$. If your
answer to a chain rule problem has no extra factor on the end, you have almost certainly dropped
the inside derivative.

## Why this note matters outside the math block

**[[Back Propagation]] is this rule and nothing else.** A [[Neural Network]] is a composition:
input goes through layer 1, its output through layer 2, and so on to a [[Loss Function]] at the
end. To ask how the loss changes when one weight deep in the middle changes, you multiply the
local rates along the path from that weight to the loss. That is a chain of $\frac{\partial
L}{\partial w}$ factors, computed right to left because that direction reuses work, which is why
the algorithm is called *backward* propagation.

```
w  →  z  →  a  →  L

∂L      ∂L   ∂a   ∂z
---  =  -- · -- · --
∂w      ∂a   ∂z   ∂w
```

With more than one variable each factor becomes a [[Partial Derivative]] and the sum over paths
matters, which is [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]. The single-variable
statement above is the whole idea; the multivariable version only adds bookkeeping.

The vanishing gradient problem is this picture read pessimistically: multiply enough factors below
$1$ along a deep chain and the product goes to zero, so the early layers stop learning. That is
why [[ReLU]] displaced [[Sigmoid|the sigmoid]] as the default [[Activation Function]].
